modules.title: Who is allowed to do what
modules.summary: The most common serious problem in web applications. It means a page or action that should be restricted can be reached by someone who should not reach it -- often just by editing the web address. It also covers a visitor tricking your site into opening web addresses they choose, which can reach private systems they could never reach themselves.

items.covers: every page and action asks visitors to sign in, or is a kind of page that is meant to be public (sign-in, health checks, webhooks)
items.title: Every private page and action requires signing in

risks.what: The action /api/admin/purge can be used by anyone, without signing in.
risks.impact: Anyone on the internet can use this address without an account. If it shows or changes anything that belongs to a particular person, they do not need to be that person to use it.
risks.fix: If this is meant to be public, nothing needs fixing: choose "This is intended". If not, make it require signing in. Best: protect the whole section of the site it belongs to, so pages added there later are protected too.
risks.fixDetail: Apply the app's sign-in middleware to POST /api/admin/purge (server/src/api.ts line 12), ideally once on the router or path prefix it sits under rather than route by route.

risks.what: The page /api/reports/:id can be opened by anyone, without signing in.
risks.impact: Anyone on the internet can use this address without an account. If it shows or changes anything that belongs to a particular person, they do not need to be that person to use it.
risks.fix: If this is meant to be public, nothing needs fixing: choose "This is intended". If not, make it require signing in. Best: protect the whole section of the site it belongs to, so pages added there later are protected too.
risks.fixDetail: Apply the app's sign-in middleware to GET /api/reports/:id (server/src/api.ts line 6), ideally once on the router or path prefix it sits under rather than route by route.

risks.what: The page /api/preview can be opened by anyone, without signing in.
risks.impact: Anyone on the internet can use this address without an account. If it shows or changes anything that belongs to a particular person, they do not need to be that person to use it.
risks.fix: If this is meant to be public, nothing needs fixing: choose "This is intended". If not, make it require signing in. Best: protect the whole section of the site it belongs to, so pages added there later are protected too.
risks.fixDetail: Apply the app's sign-in middleware to GET /api/preview (server/src/api.ts line 18), ideally once on the router or path prefix it sits under rather than route by route.

items.title: Signed-in users can only see their own records
items.question: If one customer changed a number in the web address, would they see another customer's data? Automated checks cannot tell whose record is whose -- only you know that.

items.covers: no visitor input was followed into choosing which file on your server is opened
items.title: Visitors cannot trick your site into opening files it shouldn't

items.covers: no visitor input was followed into choosing where a visitor is sent next
items.title: Links on your site cannot be used to send visitors to someone else's site

items.covers: no form saves everything a visitor sends straight into records that hold things like admin status, account balance or who owns what; records whose fields could not be found were not checked
items.title: Visitors cannot give themselves extra powers by adding hidden form fields
items.notApplicable: We couldn't find where your app describes what its saved records contain (Prisma, SQL, Mongoose, Sequelize or Drizzle), so this could not be checked. Confirm no form saves everything a visitor sends straight into a record.

items.covers: every table set up in this project's Supabase files locks each row to the people allowed to see it; tables made by hand in the Supabase dashboard were not checked
items.title: Visitors cannot read or change other people's data straight from the browser
items.notApplicable: This app doesn't use Supabase, the only database this item is about.

items.covers: every page with admin in its address checks that the visitor is an administrator
items.title: Admin pages check that the visitor is an administrator
items.question: Being signed in is not the same as being an administrator. Confirm every page and action meant for administrators checks that the visitor is one, and doesn't just hide the links.

risks.what: The admin page /api/admin/purge doesn't check that the visitor is an administrator. Any signed-in user can open it.
risks.impact: It hands out data meant only for administrators. Hiding the admin menu doesn't stop anyone: they only need the address.
risks.fix: Make the page check that the signed-in person is an administrator, and turn everyone else away.
risks.fixDetail: Add an admin-role check to POST /api/admin/purge (server/src/api.ts line 12): a `requireAdmin` middleware on every admin route, or a role test at the top of the handler that returns 403 for everyone else.

items.covers: the way your site remembers signed-in visitors is protected against actions started from other websites
items.title: Other websites cannot make signed-in visitors do things
items.question: If your site remembers who is signed in with a cookie (a small note the browser keeps), a page on another site can secretly send actions to yours while they are signed in. Confirm your site turns on protection against this (often called CSRF protection).
items.notApplicable: We couldn't see how this app remembers signed-in visitors. If it uses cookies, confirm other websites can't send actions to it for them.

items.covers: no visitor input was followed into a web address your server opens
items.title: Visitors cannot make your site open web addresses they choose

risks.what: Text in the web address (after the question mark) on the page /api/preview is used directly in choosing a web address your server then opens, and nothing checks it first.
risks.impact: Someone could make your server open addresses of their choosing, including private systems on your own network that the outside world cannot normally reach.
risks.fix: Only let your server open addresses from a list you approve, and refuse anything pointing inside your own private network -- including the special internal address hosting companies use to hand your site its passwords.
risks.fixDetail: Check the URL's host against an allowlist before fetching, and refuse private and link-local ranges (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 127/8, 169.254.169.254, ::1, fc00::/7).

items.title: Your site refuses to open addresses inside your own private network
items.question: Confirm your site refuses to open addresses inside your own private network, including the special internal address hosting companies use to hand your site its passwords.

modules.title: Settings that leave the door open
modules.summary: The code can be correct while the settings around it are not -- a setting that lets any website talk to yours, a test mode left on, a default password never changed.

items.covers: the setup file (Dockerfile) that packages your app runs it as an ordinary user, not with full administrator rights
items.title: Your app doesn't run with full control of the computer it's on
items.notApplicable: This app isn't packaged with a Dockerfile, so there is no container to check.

items.covers: the setup files used to start the live app don't switch on test or debug mode; settings in a hosting service's dashboard were not checked
items.title: Test mode is off where the app runs for real
items.notApplicable: We couldn't see how your live site is started. If you use a hosting service (Vercel, Netlify, Render and similar), check its settings show production mode.

items.covers: your app doesn't accept behind-the-scenes requests from every website
items.title: Only your own website can talk to your app behind the scenes

items.covers: your site asks visitors' browsers to switch on their built-in protections
items.title: Your site turns on the browser's built-in safety features
items.question: Confirm your site asks browsers to switch on their built-in protections (called security headers). It costs nothing and closes a whole group of browser attacks.

risks.what: Your site doesn't ask visitors' browsers to switch on their built-in protections (security headers).
risks.impact: Browsers can refuse to show your site inside someone else's page, or to run code from places you did not approve, but only when your site asks. Without that, a small problem elsewhere becomes a much bigger one.
risks.fix: Add the one standard line that switches these protections on. It needs no setup to be useful.
risks.fixDetail: Add `app.use(secureHeaders())` (from "hono/secure-headers") near the top of server/src/api.ts.

items.covers: your setup file (docker-compose) doesn't open the database to the outside world
items.title: The database is not reachable from the internet
items.question: Confirm your database can only be reached by your own app, not from the internet.
items.notApplicable: This project has no docker-compose setup file, so how the database is reached could not be seen. If your database is hosted somewhere, check in its settings that only your app can connect to it.

modules.title: Building blocks you did not write
modules.summary: Your application is built from packages (code written by other people), and built and published by automated tools. A flaw or a break-in anywhere along that chain ends up inside your application, even if your own code is perfect.

items.covers: every public package your app installs, against OSV.dev's list of known security flaws
items.title: None of the packages your app uses has a publicly known security flaw
items.question: If this could not be checked automatically, ask your AI assistant to run `npm audit` and fix what it reports.
items.notApplicable: Checking packages against the public list of known flaws is switched off. Ask your AI assistant to run your package manager's audit command instead.

items.covers: no package is named one letter away from one of about 100 popular packages
items.title: No package looks like a misspelled copy of a popular one
items.notApplicable: No package list (package.json) was found, so there are no package names to check.

items.title: None of your packages is abandoned or comes from an unofficial place
items.question: A package that has not been updated in years will not be fixed when a flaw is found in it. Check the ones your app relies on most.

items.covers: every package in package.json is set to one exact version
items.title: Your app always installs the exact package versions you tested
items.question: Confirm each package is set to one exact version rather than "this version or newer", so the code you tested is the code that goes live.
items.notApplicable: No package list (package.json) was found, so this could not be checked.

items.covers: a lockfile is saved with your code
items.title: Your app keeps a record of every package version it installs (a lockfile)
items.question: Confirm a lockfile is saved with your code. Without one, two installs of the same code can pull different package versions.
items.notApplicable: No package list (package.json) was found, so there are no package versions to record.

items.title: Only people you trust can change the automatic steps that build and publish your site
items.question: These automatic steps (for example GitHub Actions) usually hold the passwords to your live site. Check who on GitHub can change them.

modules.title: Protecting passwords, keys, and personal data
modules.summary: Covers secrets that should never be readable -- passwords, and the keys that give access to other services -- and private data, both while it is being sent and while it is stored.

items.covers: no keys, passwords, or sign-in secrets are written into your code
items.title: No keys or passwords are written into the code

risks.what: an LLM provider API key is written directly into your code (server/src/api.ts line 24).
risks.impact: Anyone who can read your code can use it as you. Deleting the line later doesn't help, because GitHub keeps every old version -- the key has to be cancelled and replaced.
risks.fix: First cancel this key on the provider's website (it is already exposed), then make a new one and keep it in your hosting service's secret settings, not in the code.
risks.fixDetail: Revoke the credential with the provider, issue a new one, read it from an environment variable, and remove the literal from the code.

items.covers: passwords are scrambled with bcrypt or argon2, methods built for passwords
items.title: Passwords are scrambled in a way that's hard to undo
items.question: Passwords must never be saved as typed, or scrambled with a quick method like MD5 or SHA-256. Confirm yours use argon2id or bcrypt, which are slow on purpose so guessing takes too long to be worth it.
items.notApplicable: This app doesn't seem to handle passwords.

items.covers: no page sends complete user records, scrambled passwords included, to the browser
items.title: Stored passwords are never sent back to the browser
items.question: When a page loads user records, confirm the stored password is left out of what is sent -- even scrambled, it can be cracked.
items.notApplicable: We couldn't find a description of user records with a password, so this couldn't be checked. If your app stores passwords, confirm pages that load users leave the password out.

items.title: You know what personal data this application stores
items.question: List what you collect that would matter if it leaked -- names, emails, payment details, health information. Some of it carries legal obligations.

modules.title: Visitor input being treated as instructions
modules.summary: Happens when something a visitor types is pasted into a command, a database request, or a page, and gets treated as an instruction rather than as text. This is what ShipBrace checks most thoroughly.

items.covers: no visitor input was followed into a database request
items.title: Visitors can't change what your database does by typing special text

risks.what: Part of the web address on the page /api/reports/:id is used directly in a database query (a request your app sends to its database), and nothing checks it first.
risks.impact: Someone could read, change, or delete anything in your database -- including other people's accounts and personal information -- by typing carefully chosen text into your site.
risks.fix: Send the visitor's text to the database separately from the question your app is asking it, so the database always treats it as plain text and never as part of the question.
risks.fixDetail: Use query parameters instead of joining the value into the SQL text: the tagged `sql` template for postgres, or `?` placeholders with an argument array for mysql2.

location.excerpt: const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM reports WHERE id = ${id}`);

risks.evidence: c.req.param("id") → id → rows → `SELECT * FROM reports WHERE id = ${id}`

items.covers: no visitor input was followed into a computer command or into code your app runs
items.title: Visitor input is never run as a command or as code

risks.what: Something the visitor sends from their browser on the action /api/admin/purge is used directly in a command run on the computer that hosts your site, and nothing checks it first.
risks.impact: Someone could run their own commands on the machine hosting your site, which usually means full control of it.
risks.fix: Never build a computer command out of a visitor's text. Better still, use a ready-made package that does the job without running a command at all.
risks.fixDetail: Pass the program and its arguments as a separate array (`execFile(cmd, [arg])` or `spawn` without `shell: true`) instead of building one string for `exec`, so the shell never interprets characters inside the value.

items.covers: no visitor input was followed into a page without being made safe first
items.title: Visitors can't sneak their own code into your pages

unproven.what: Text is put into the page without being made safe first (app/src/Profile.tsx line 4).
unproven.why: Pages normally show text as plain text, but this line switches that off. If the text ever comes from a visitor, their code runs in other visitors' browsers and can take over their accounts.
unproven.check: Show the value as plain text. If it really has to include formatting, clean it with a trusted cleaning package first.
unproven.checkDetail: Render it escaped: `{value}` in React instead of dangerouslySetInnerHTML; Hono's html`` helper instead of a plain template; `<%= %>` not `<%- %>` in EJS. If it must be HTML, run it through DOMPurify first.

items.covers: in each page's code, a visitor's text never goes to a well-known AI service (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Vercel AI SDK, LangChain) whose answer is then used to change data, run commands, open addresses or send messages, or that is given tools; AI code in other places was not followed
items.title: A visitor's text cannot steer what an AI feature does
items.notApplicable: This app seems to use an AI service in a way this check can't follow. Confirm a visitor's text can't make the AI's answer change data, run commands or send messages.

items.covers: no uploaded XML was followed into libxmljs with the setting that pulls in other files switched on; other XML tools, and settings written elsewhere, were not checked
items.title: Uploaded XML files can't make your site reveal its own private files

modules.title: Gaps in how the feature was designed
modules.summary: Some problems are not mistakes in the code -- the code does exactly what it was asked to. These are gaps in what was asked for, so no automated tool can find them. They need your knowledge of how the product is supposed to work.

items.title: You have thought about how someone would deliberately misuse this
items.question: For each thing your app does, ask: what would someone gain by doing this a thousand times, out of order, or with values you did not expect?

items.covers: something limits how often one person can use your pages and actions
items.title: Nobody can repeat an action thousands of times a minute
items.question: Anything that costs you money, sends a message, or checks a password should refuse to run thousands of times a minute for one person. Confirm which of your actions have a limit.

risks.what: None of your 3 pages and actions limits how often one person can use it.
risks.impact: One person can then use any of them thousands of times a minute -- guessing passwords, running up costs on anything you pay for per use, or slowing the site down for everyone.
risks.fix: Add a limit on how often one person can use each action, with a stricter one on signing in and on anything that costs you money.
risks.fixDetail: Add rate-limiting middleware (express-rate-limit for Express, hono-rate-limiter for Hono) to all routes, with a tighter limit on sign-in and costly routes.

items.covers: no page sends back every row of a table at once, with no filter or limit (Express or Hono pages using Mongoose, Sequelize, Prisma or plain SQL; Drizzle and Next.js pages were not checked)
items.title: Lists sent to visitors have a maximum size

items.covers: every upload feature built with multer sets a size limit; other upload tools were not checked
items.title: Uploads have a size limit
items.notApplicable: We didn't find an upload feature we know how to check (only multer is checked). If visitors can upload files, confirm there's a size limit.

items.title: Important rules are checked by your site, not just in the visitor's browser
items.question: Anything checked only in the browser can be skipped entirely -- the browser belongs to the visitor, not to you. Prices, limits, and permissions must be checked again by your site.

modules.title: Proving who someone is
modules.summary: Covers signing in, staying signed in, and signing out. Weaknesses here let someone become another user, which makes every other permission check meaningless.

items.covers: the visitor's sign-in pass is never kept where code running on the page can read it
items.title: Your sign-in pass can't be stolen by code running on the page

items.covers: sign-in passes are given an expiry time
items.title: Sign-ins expire, and signing out really signs you out
items.question: Confirm a sign-in does not last forever, and that signing out really ends it on your site rather than only in the browser.
items.notApplicable: This app doesn't seem to sign people in, so there are no sign-ins to expire.

items.title: Repeated failed sign-ins are slowed down or blocked
items.question: Without a limit, someone can try millions of passwords against one account. Confirm repeated failures are slowed down, locked, or challenged.

items.title: Password reset cannot be used to take over an account
items.question: Reset links must expire, work only once, and be sent only to the email already on the account. This is the most commonly abused way into an account.

modules.title: Trusting data that could have been tampered with
modules.summary: Covers data and code your application accepts as genuine without checking -- a script loaded from someone else's site, a cookie the visitor could edit, data arriving from another system.

items.title: Data from other services is checked before your app uses it
items.question: Data arriving from another system is no more trustworthy than something a visitor typed. Confirm it is checked to be what you expect before your app uses it.

items.covers: no visitor input was followed into node-serialize, funcster, or js-yaml's unsafe loading, tools that can turn data into code; other tools were not checked
items.title: Data from outside can't turn into code your app runs

items.covers: every address where another service sends you updates (a webhook) sits in code that checks each message's signature
items.title: Messages from other services are checked to be genuine
items.notApplicable: We didn't find an address where other services send this app updates (a webhook). If it has one, confirm each message's signature is checked before the app acts on it.

items.title: Code loaded from other websites can't be swapped without you noticing
items.question: If your pages load code straight from another website, whoever runs that site can change what runs on yours. Confirm each one is locked to an exact version with a safety check (called subresource integrity), or hosted on your own site.

items.title: Anything that comes back from the visitor's browser is double-checked
items.question: Cookies, hidden form fields, and saved settings pass through the visitor's browser, where they can be edited. Confirm anything you rely on -- a role, a price, an account number -- is either signed so changes are noticed, or looked up again by your site.

modules.title: Noticing when something goes wrong
modules.summary: If an attack succeeds and nobody notices, it continues. The average break-in goes unnoticed for months. This module is about being able to tell that something happened, and when -- and making sure someone is told.

items.title: Sign-ins, failed sign-ins, and refused actions are written down
items.question: Confirm your app records who signed in, what failed, and what was refused. Without it there is no way to work out what happened after an incident.

items.covers: no password, sign-in pass, or key is written into your app's activity records, and the database tool doesn't record every request
items.title: Your app's activity records (logs) never contain passwords or keys
items.question: Activity records are copied, sent to other services, and read by more people than your database. Confirm nothing sensitive is written into them.

items.title: Someone would actually see an alert
items.question: Records nobody reads aren't monitoring. Decide who gets told when something goes wrong, and for what.

modules.title: When something unexpected happens
modules.summary: Errors are where applications behave least predictably. A check that crashes might let everyone through, an error message might reveal how the system is built, and one malformed request might bring the whole thing down.

items.covers: your own code never sends error details to visitors, and you have your own error page
items.title: Error messages don't show visitors how your site is built
items.question: The technical details of an error (file names, code, database messages) tell an attacker how your site is built. Confirm visitors see a short message, and the detail goes into your private records instead.

items.title: When a check breaks, the answer is no
items.question: If a permission check, a payment, or a sign-in lookup fails with an error, the safe outcome is to refuse. Confirm none of your error handling quietly carries on as if the check had passed.

items.title: One unexpected request cannot crash or freeze the application
items.question: Confirm unexpected errors are caught and answered with a short message, and that oversized or broken requests are refused early instead of using up memory or hanging.
